title: Soft Contamination Means Benchmarks Test Shallow Generalization
claim: A two-stage workflow first detects semantic duplicates of benchmark items in training data, then finetunes models on them to measure effects.
layout: 2 color-coded rows of boxes, left-to-right, with connecting arrows and a dashed link
description: A flow diagram of rounded boxes joined by arrows, in two color-coded groups. The top row, labelled CONTAMINATION DETECTION, uses blue/lavender boxes. It starts with a gray box for OLMo-3 training corpora and runs through embedding the corpus and benchmarks, cosine similarity matching, LLM annotation with Gemini 3 Flash, and a final Gemini grader. It ends in a gray output box for contamination prevalence. The lower section, labelled FINETUNING EXPERIMENTS, uses red/salmon boxes. A gray box of benchmark datasets (MBPP, CodeForces, MuSR, Zebra) feeds up into the embedding step and right into generating synthetic duplicates. Those duplicates feed LoRA finetuning of OLMo-3 and a separate ecological finetune. A dashed blue arrow from the final grader goes to the finetuning box. Outputs are gray boxes for evaluating OLMo-3 and cross-model evaluation on Qwen. Gray marks inputs and outputs. Each box has a bold title and a smaller subtitle.
caption: Our full pipeline from input data to experimental outcomes.
abstract: Training on benchmark test items is a classic way to overestimate generalization to unseen problems. Standard decontamination methods miss semantic duplicates (SemDs): training items equivalent in content to a test item, but distant in string space. We call training on such items soft contamination; when the resulting gains extend to held-out items of the same benchmark (but not to related benchmarks), we call the result shallow generalization. We first embed Olmo 3's entire post-training dataset and search it for SemDs of benchmark items; we then finetune Olmo 3 and Qwen models on natural and synthetic semantic duplicates. We find (1) that soft contamination is widespread: the Olmo corpus contains SemDs of 76% of the CodeForces test set and 100% of MBPP's; (2) that finetuning on SemDs of a benchmark raises accuracy on its held-out items by up to 22pp in controlled experiments and 10-11pp at realistic contamination rates, though the effect varies across benchmarks; (3) that the gains from training on SemDs mostly do not transfer to conceptually similar benchmarks, i.e. we find shallow generalization; (4) that finetuning on items with similar embeddings that are not SemDs produces no such gain, indicating that the mechanism is not mere topical similarity; and (5) that at realistic contamination rates, soft contamination can raise held-out performance about as much as exact duplicates (or more). Benchmark gains here are therefore confounded - in a way that standard decontamination does not address.
